chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
title: The Black Tie: Pee Wee declines the Australian Ambassador's show
summary: Freeman recalls Mary's death, an invitation to show Pee Wee's paintings, and Pee Wee skipping it for lack of a tuxedo; talent moved into another art.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yes, and PeeWee, now think, PeeWee -- Rutger*s University gave PeeWee a show, now we got a call. Before Mary died, Mary died about a year before PeeWee.
Yes, nine months to a year.
We all went to Mary's funeral. I didn't go to PeeWee's, I was away or something, but went to Mary's.

Now, Mary called me and told me that she got a telephone call from the Australian Ambassador who was in Washington and he wanted to put on -- he was putting on a show of painters from New Zealand, Tasmanian and Australia and they wanted to include PeeWee's works. And would he come. It was to be a black tie affair.

Now, I wrote a short story about this, called The Black Tie, and so Mary said 'I don't think PeeWee wants to go,' and I said, 'Well, let me talk to him.' So I got PeeWee on the phone and I bawled him out and I said, 'PeeWee, you have got to go to that thing,' and he said, 'Bud, I can't. I haven't got a tuxedo.' And I said, 'Well, for Christ's sake, get one, do you realize this will launch you into becoming a world renowned painter?'

Well, alas, PeeWee did not go and the final line of the thing, I say, I think truly that PeeWee did not think of himself as being a painter and I said, 'He could have fooled the Australian Ambassador,' and that's the tale.

It was said, because he would have had this luxurious life. Of course, he was doing well, making money and just picking his jobs and getting well paid. He had become an idol, you see, around the world. PeeWee Russell, the world knew him backwards.
George Wein, of course, was devoted to him.

Well, he was, yes, so anyway here was PeeWee now a painter. Now, isn't it interesting that this transference of -- remember, Ernie Anderson said, 'What do you think it is?' I said, 'Well, it's a transference of intelligence and talent into another idiom of art.'

Because through all this haze of being -- all the years of being drunk and falling down -- not falling down, but just being so nervous and you never knew that the man was seeing things, and here he was, not knowing that he was so aware, and we didn't know that he was so aware of this art, because some of the paintings are excellent, or maybe many aren't.
But at any rate, I think that people were, as I said, more interested in the idea that a jazz musician could become a painter than anything else. This was a big story to them.
